text.content: 4: Technology & Equipment ife beyond Earth would be impossible without technology. It allowed humans to escape the gravity well of Earth, to establish a foothold in the expanse of our solar system, and to establish colonies on the worlds of distant stars. In the era of The Expanse, technology is so omnipresent it sometimes fades into the background—until a minute failure leads to catastrophe, reminding everyone just how critical it is. The future is full of wonders—expert systems running on evermore-powerful computers; missing eyes and limbs replaced with cybernetic implants; city-sized Void ships that travel the solar system and beyond; and new technologies, such as carbon silicate lace plating, derived from the protomolecule. Technology is also old and ubiquitous. The majority of ships are decades old, built using technology that hasn’t changed in generations. Technology on stations is often even older, and the colony worlds beyond the ring gates often favor the old and familiar over cutting-edge tech because it’s cheap and easier to replace. Technology is familiar, reliable, and useful. The equipment listed in this chapter runs the gamut of weapons and armor to tools and items essential to survival in The Expanse. Whether the crew is relying on their vac suits in the event of a hull breach or their weapons to fend off harm, having the right equipment can make the difference between life and death.

Humans are tool-dependent creatures, and a lot of what constitutes gear or equipment are the various tools and devices we use to make life easier. Although the gear in The Expanse has gotten more sophisticated in a number of ways, it still largely serves the same function.

Some items are restricted by legality, either requiring special permits or licensing or being restricted to only active-duty security or military personnel. Other items are restricted by rarity. While —Leviathan Falls you can buy a new hand terminal at almost any station in the system, finding a custom-made item with all of the qualities you want may require you to shop in the right places.

An Expanse GM can use access and availability in two ways:

First, a GM can restrict the Player Characters from buying something even if they happen to have sufficient Income or are feeling lucky with their next Income test. Feel free to tell them that the item is not available, either at all or in the place where they are looking. Or maybe there is a good reason the item has gone missing, which leads to the next option. Second, availability, or the lack thereof, can make an excellent story hook. If a PC really wants something, dangling an opportunity to get it in front of them is a great way to get the crew involved in a story—or makes an excellent reward if they do well. Even if it’s nigh-impossible to buy a suit of military-grade power armor (even on the black market), you can still arrange things in an adventure to give a character a shot at acquiring some, provided they’re willing to put up with looking after it.

Item Qualities and Flaws

Not all things are made equally. Much like characters, they have their focuses and talents. Some items may have qualities that reflect certain improvements over common items of that type, or they may have flaws, which are drawbacks or problems compared to common items. Being able to afford flawless equipment, much less items of high-quality, is a common goal for Expanse characters when they are starting out and have to make do with that they have. As a general guideline, each quality an item has increases its Cost for income tests to acquire it by +1, while each flaw decreases Cost by −1. The GM decides if a particular quality or flaw can apply to a particular item, as not all of them may be appropriate. If a quality or flaw is limited to a particular type of item, it generally says so in the description. Some special qualities and flaws are listed alongside specific types of items in this chapter as well.

Item Qualities

DURABLE The item is built to last. Under normal conditions, it lasts twice as long, and for tests involving damaging it, it has a +2 Toughness.

EFFECTIVE The item works better than a regular item of its type, gaining a +1 bonus to one of its abilities, such as damage, armor bonus, or some other ability used for outcome or effectiveness, but not for tests (see Fine, following, for that quality), or a 50% improvement in overall output. A Very Effective item has two qualities and provides a +2 bonus or a 100% improvement.

FAST The item works fast. It takes half the usual time to use a regular item of its type. For something using during action time, the character gains a +2 bonus to initiative when using the item (see Initiative in Chapter 5).

FAVORED STUNT The item is either especially well-suited for performing a particular stunt, granting a −1 SP modifier to its cost, or else the item grants access to a unique stunt the character can perform while wielding or using it. Each favored stunt is a separate quality and an item can have more than one.

FINE The item’s quality is such that the character gains a +1 bonus to tests for using or wielding it. Very Fine items have two qualities and provide a +2 bonus.

IMPRESSIVE The item’s quality is clearly apparent, providing a +1 bonus to social and roleplaying tests where such things are noteworthy, such as trying to make a good impression while wearing an Impressive outfit or intimidating someone with an Impressive weapon. Very Impressive items have two qualities and provide a +2 bonus.

LIGHT The item is lighter and more compact than normal, reducing any penalty to Dexterity and Speed it normally imposes by 1. Very Light items have two qualities and reduced penalties by 2.

UNTRACEABLE Some items—frequently weapons, but not exclusively—can be coated with a resin of digestive enzymes that prevent the object from accumulating fingerprints, DNA traces, or other common types of trace evidence that law enforcement uses to find out who used the object. Touching such an object causes a minor, harmless burning sensation.

Item Flaws

FRAGILE The item wasn’t made to take much punishment. A deliberate attempt to break it always succeeds. Furthermore, when a test to use the item fails, and the Drama Die is 3 or less, the item breaks.

HEAVY The item is heavier or bulkier than normal, imposing a 1 penalty to the Dexterity and Speed of a character carrying or wearing it. Very heavy items have two flaws and impose a 2 penalty to Dexterity and Speed.

INEFFECTIVE The item can’t inflict damage as easily as a proper weapon, imposing a −1 or −2 penalty to damage rolls, with a minimum damage roll of 1.

POOR The overall poor quality of the item imposes a −1 penalty to tests using or wielding it. Very Poor items have two flaws and impose a −2 penalty.

SHODDY The item’s flaws are glaringly apparent, imposing a −1 penalty to social and roleplaying tests where such things are noteworthy, such as trying to intimidate someone with a Shoddy weapon, or make a good first impression in a Shoddy outfit. The GM may adjust the penalty, depending on the circumstances, but it is always negative.

SLOW The item works, but not fast. It takes twice as much time to use as a regular item of its type. For something that can be used with a major action during action time, a Slow item requires a Ready action after it is used each time to prepare it to be used again.

UNRELIABLE The item works…most of the time. When a test involving the item fails and the Drama Die is a 3 or less, the item stops working. If the item does not require a test to use, the GM should roll 3d6 when the item needs to work. On a total roll of 10 or less where the Drama Die is a 3 or less, the item stops working. Getting an Unreliable item working again takes either an interlude to fix it or, during action time, a TN 13 challenge test with a success threshold of 10 and a time increment of 1 round.

Generally, any character with Income above 0 will have at least their own hand terminal and access to a local network unless they are under some kind of restrictions (imprisoned, for example). Stationary computer terminals are a part of every ship, workplace, and home, and their quality varies based on where they are found. A new hand terminal is generally an Income TN of 11 but can be higher based on quality and availability. Most computer-related tests are Intelligence (Technology), although no test is required for routine operation of a terminal to access unrestricted files, search networks, place calls, or send messages, and so forth. The GM may apply a modifier to any required test based on the quality of the terminal, the local network, and the character’s access.

Communications

The actual communications connections between devices are often simple radio, though feeds broadcast this way are open to anyone with an antenna listening at the proper frequency. Private communications require laser arrays for tightbeam transmissions only receivable where the laser is aimed. The greater the distance between sender and receiver, the harder it is to keep the broadcast laser focused. To keep the laser as tight as possible across enormous distances, equally enormous and powerful comm lasers like the one aboard Tycho Station must be used. Tightbeam transmissions also require comprehensive knowledge of the target’s position, speed, and trajectory. To help tightbeams maintain coherence, relays are set up across the solar system to receive a transmission laser before rebroadcasting it toward the intended recipient. Though these relay services work hard to maintain the trust of those who use them, corporations and intelligence agencies maintain private relays with onboard drop sites, moving in orbits unknown to anyone but their owners. In order to be accessed, they require not just the encryption keys necessary for communication, but also intimate knowledge of the relay’s exactly position at any given time.

Communications Networks

All these devices and systems communicate via a constantly shifting network of connections. Every element has its own network address, identifying it so commands and data can be transmitted to and from it no matter where it connects. Sometimes these elements are part of a simple local network, such as a hand terminal paired with its earbuds or a family’s closed network of home terminals, and keeping them isolated is a simple matter. But as soon as an element of the network is connected to a network bridge or an open comm array, it becomes part of a larger network. Passwords, magnetic security cards, and biometric locks are common security measures, as are simple expert systems for networks with sufficient processing power. However, hackers and the powerful expert systems employed by governments and corporations are formidable enough to penetrate nearly any connected network given access and time, so those who truly have data to hide do their best to keep it discon-

Given the physical isolation experienced by ships in the depths of space and the small populations of most established communities, most people are happy to keep a network connection open to communicate with others at a distance. The public network is made up of a seemingly infinite number of information feeds, from Martian planetary news feeds to entertainment feeds of live music and commentary. Some are open feeds intended for a broad audience, while others are “narrowcasts” created for a specific audience and some - times limited to only those who have the password or paid for access. Some feeds allow users to participate, welcoming them into discussion groups or singles circles for those seeking romantic relationships. When bandwidth becomes a concern, feeds can limit themselves to audio or text-only content. It can an overwhelming amount of information, so many terminals come preinstalled with simple feed managers to help curate feeds and offer only the content of the user’s choice. The user’s personal correspondence comes via feed connections as well, and feed managers help ensure they don’t miss important communications—and can block unwelcome messages while flagging high-priority or secure ones. Like all forms of communication, networks are limited by the speed of light in transmitting and receiving data. On board a ship, station, or on a planet or moon, this delay is too brief to be noticed, but it can extend to hours out in the system. Therefore, network software tends to queue data-traffic for trans - mission whenever there is an opportunity, updating the local network data as transmissions are received. See Communications, following, and System Communication and Travel Times in Chapter 6 for additional information.

Partitions

Partitions are portions of computer memory on a device or in a larger archive, and a user typically has access to multiple partitions based on their needs to help keep their data secure. A hand terminal has a device partition on its own hardware, but it can be connected to a family partition on a home terminal, a local partition maintained by a ship, city, or other organization, or even a public partition shared by many users. These partitions can be open or locked with a password, and the files placed into them can similarly be left open or given multiple layers of security. When data is moved around on nearby parts of a network, individual files are manipulated as easily as if they were on the user’s local terminal, but when data is moved across a connection where broadcast times are measured in significant fractions of a light-second, users sometimes take the time to assemble data into broadcast packets of related data. Distant or isolated partitions are called drop sites, often used for long-term storage of data or the passing of data between anonymous users; a “black drop site” was once found running on a terminal with a partition attached to an independent power source and mounted with a broadcast array on the exterior of an isolated asteroid. The truly paranoid or security conscious don’t trust their data to any communications network, maintaining an “air gap” and physically moving it from one place to another on physical media like a hand terminal or memory wafer.
This section provides details on a wide array of equipment available to characters including emergency equipment, electronic and spy gadgets, environment suits, drones, mechs, weapons, and armor.

Battery power in The Expanse, being as efficient as it is, will allow devices to function without the need for recharge or replacements for as long as it serves the narrative.

Computer Terminal Cost 7

Standard computer terminals range from portable networked data pads to fixed location terminals set on a desk- or tabletop, or mounted on an articulated swing arm at the workstation, particularly on board a ship or station. Terminals can be paired with a stylus used to draw or write on the screen, processed by software able to turn handwriting into plain text or calligraphy. Users can use gestures to “flick” or throw files across the network to nearby devices as easily as tossing a physical object. Earbuds or headsets allow a wearer to privately listen to audio feeds or communicate and control the terminal subvocally via built-in microphones. Keyboards are available for those who prefer them as a form of input, and many professions have their own unique keyboard layouts, like the programing keyboards preferred by software engineers and hackers. Hand Terminal Cost 8

Almost everyone has a hand terminal—a palm-sized portable computer used to display information or run programs. Hand terminals have onboard processing and memory, allowing them to run “simple experts” to help organize the user’s daily life, play games and other entertainment software, or let the user read books, listen to music, or watch videos from the network or its internal library. A hand terminal can be used via controls displayed on its touchscreen, or through voice recognition, letting the user give it commands in everyday language. Hand terminals are cheap and ubiquitously available, and when one is lost or damaged, it is easily replaced, with the user’s profile reloaded from a partitioned backup.

Motion Tracker Cost 15

This is a handheld device with a screen that displays any detected movement within 10 meters. The tracker can sense movement around corners to a limited degree, but not on the other side of sealed compartments. The user can pair the display to one or more hand terminals.

Night Vision Goggles Cost 14

This piece of fashionable spyware uses illumination enhancement and computer modeling software to eliminate attack roll modifiers and other penalties related to darkness. Spacesuit helmets can also be outfitted with nightvision technology. (Add +3 to the cost of a spacesuit for this upgrade.)

Signal Jammer Cost 13

Handheld signal jammers can disrupt radio communications within 100 meters, preventing readable signals from either entering or leaving the area. This does not block tightbeam transmissions, which use lasers instead of radio. Operators of radios within the device’s radius can detect that a signal jammer is in use.

Thermal Goggles Cost 12

These goggles allow their wearers to see heat signatures, allowing them to locate targets that would otherwise be invisible or to gain valuable sensory information (such as where a suit of powered armor’s energy source is located, or if someone is running a fever). Spacesuit helmets can also be outfitted with thermal technology. (Add +2 to the cost of a spacesuit for this upgrade.)

Rescue-And-Recovery Kit Cost14

Commonly carried on passenger ships, shuttles, and search-and-rescue craft, these kits (also known as R-and-R packs) look like massive backpacks. They contain two emergency vac suits, a collapsible emergency airlock, a single-use cutting torch, a distress beacon, and a medical kit.

Thruster Pack Cost 11

While vac suits have the ability to use brief bursts of air to impart a limited amount of thrust, most standard environment suits do not. In either case, these thruster packs provide greater mobility and duration for travel in a vacuum. The total distance or duration available depends on how long each burst of air is (which also determines acceleration), but conservative use allows about two hours of continuous maneuvering. Thrusters are controlled by an on-board computer that calculates trajectories and use of reaction mass, making most short trips relatively safe and easy.

Vac Suit Cost 11

Vac suits are heavier space suits that have corrugated joints connecting hard?ened plastic segments, helmets with thick transparent faceplates, and connections for separate air-supply units. Despite a vac suit’s bulk and complaints that they’re poorly heated and cooled, they’re quite effective at keeping the wearer alive and functional. They feature integrated magnetic boots and communications rigs, along with water tanks and food supplies running to dispensers inside the helmet. They’re also easy to repair, with some vac suits passed down from one generation to another among Belter mining families

Drones are semi-autonomous vehicles. They’re commonly built as small aerostats with propellers that allow them to hover and fly like helicopters in atmosphere, or they’re given micro-thrusters that let them “teakettle” maneuver in microgravity, with or without an atmosphere. Some drones are ground bound, using either tracked or wheeled drives or multiple robotic legs to maneuver. Those designed for microgravity have magnetic adhesion, much like a DRONES

Advertising Drone Cost 14

One of the simplest of drones, this model plays audio or video ads to promote products, services, or even govern ments or political movements.

Crowd-Suppression Drone Cost 15

This variant of the security drone employs crowd-suppres sion rounds (see the new Suppression quality under Ranged Weapon Qualities) to pacify groups of combatants, typically civilians during a riot.

Freight Drone Cost 14

Closet-sized freight drones are common for shipping cargo between locations in space, such as from one habitat to another, or from station to ship. In times of emergency, freight drones have served as makeshift escape capsules, as they have room enough for a person though not comfortably, and not always safely.

Loader Drone Cost 14

Although no drone can lift a large amount of weight individu ally, in large numbers, they are formidable. They attach to an object using strong but lightweight cables and maneuver collectively using networked programming. An advanced variant called a transport drone is designed to move larger or more unwieldy objects, potentially across greater distances.

Relay Drone Cost 14

Communication focused relay drones convey radar or tight beam laser signals from one or more sources to one or more destinations, and they can do so on a complex, ever changing, pre programmed flight path. This can be for typical signal propagation or to help obscure one or both ends of a transmission circuit.

The Danger of Drones

While drones can be useful and a fun part of a story, if care isn’t taken, they can also remove the player characters from the action. If players start to rely too much on drones, you may want to limit their use. After all, this is a game about the player characters, not drones. Talk with your players about saving drones for an important scene, or if they are resistant, use the Churn to wreak havoc with their drones, or have enemies or wildlife target their drones. Some places may also interfere with drone reception, making them difficult to use.

Sampling Drone Cost 14

One of a variety of drones created for scientific use, these drones collect samples from their environment using sampling arms in a variety of sizes and configurations—some can cut stone, others can scoop up insects, and still others can take blood samples. The body of the drone is reconfigu-rable, made of a network of flexible and movable connectors.

Security Drone Cost 16

The typical security drone used by police and security forces has audio/video monitoring capabilities as well as either a light slugthrower or stun pistol. Some advanced models add motion trackers, night vision, or other sensory upgrades. Operators can talk through the drone’s speakers, and the drone itself can also issue programmed warnings in its own mechanical voice.

Surveillance Drone Cost 15

Spying is one of the most popular uses for drones, as miniature machines can reach ideal snooping points much more easily than human bodies can. These drones are capable of recording targets using audio, video, radio, and, even more invasively, with x-ray scanners, thermal imagers, and more. They typically report their findings using either tightbeam laser (to avoid interception) or in person via direct data upload.

Mechs are bulky exoskeletons, usually offering no actual life support, but considerably amplifying the wearer’s strength. Mechs range from a simple arrangement strapped over the user’s shoulders, with mechanical, articulated arms, to an egg-shaped open cage with the wearer strapped into its center, equipped with four articulated limbs that provide stability and utility, each limb ending in a foot that can be rotated back to deploy a variety of cutting and welding tools. Mechs also have tether points where crewmates can connect themselves to be carried to and from a labor site, and where loads of parts, salvage, or ore can be stowed. most are multi-purpose and at least have mounting points for maneuvering jets. In space, mechs use small jets of compressed nitrogen to maneuver and electromagnetic feet to attach to surfaces. Such mechs often include a protected compartment that eliminates the need for a vac suit; these mechs are sometimes referred to as “mech suits.” Some mechs are operable by remote control or have the ability to be automated in a limited way, though this is more commonly done with drones. Industrial mechs are often equipped with cameras and x-ray scanners. Large spacecraft that make heavy use of mechs (such as ice haulers) often incorporate external storage sheds that can hold a dozen or more mechs. Construction and labor mechs provide a substantial Strength bonus (usually +10), which affects Strength (Might) tests. Full-sized mechs are equivalent to vehicles, with their own Speed stat, and offer a measure of cover to someone strapped in, generally enough for a +2 armor bonus. See Vehicles in Combat in Chapter 5 for additional useful guidelines for these types of mechs.

Cost 16

Construction mechs come in two sizes; the smaller variety is “standard” mech-sized, designed to hold a human driver. These safety-yellow-and-orange mechs are used for the construction and repair of spacecraft and habitats, featuring welders, industrial-strength work lights, and numerous other tools. Spaceships often keep a stock of these held in racks along with vac suits. Construction mech drivers must wear their own environment suits, as the mech itself is only an enclosure with straps and spider-like limbs.

Cost 18

The larger variety of construction mech is bigger than a house and takes a generally humanoid shape—plus several extra limbs and protrusions. These mechs are used for similar purposes as their smaller kin but done on a larger scale. Giant construction mechs are often automated.

Cost 15

Also called a half-mech or half-suit mech, this mech variant is a framework that envelops a person’s upper half to provide the functionality of a salvage mech. The user straps it across their back before fitting it over the chest and arms, but it does not cover the legs. Like a standard salvage mech, the half-mech incorporates a cutting torch and metal claws that impart great strength for tasks such as gripping, bending, and tearing metal. The user controls these metal hands by using waldoes in the mech’s forearms. When folded up, this yellow exoskeleton is small and light enough to carry easily. It can provide a degree of protection in combat, but maneuvering it in a fight is unwieldy.

Cost 16

A variant of loader mech, the squat, blocky, lifting mechs are designed to carry much heavier loads than standard loaders work with, such as slabs of ferrocrete. Unlike loader mechs, which spend most of their time moving uniform cargo containers, lifting mechs are also better-suited to handle nonstandard loads.

Loader Mech Cost 16

Also known as loading mechs, these are common industrial mechs used to haul large amounts of cargo with their claws and magnetic clamps, especially in standardized cargo containers. At large spaceports, one can see literal swarms of loader mechs and drones unloading cargo from ships, often in automated mode. Unlike construction mechs and salvage mechs, loaders are not enclosed, so when operating in a vacuum, their drivers must strap in while wearing a separate environment suit. Loader mechs are commonly available for rent at most spaceports.

Salvage Mech Cost 16

Sometimes called demolition mechs, salvage mechs are one of the most common mechs in use at spaceports and other places where spacecraft operate. These mechs excel at both making repairs and slicing up large masses, usually asteroids, ice masses, and parts of ships. Salvage mechs are bright yellow with a vacuum-sealed, egg-shaped cage for the driver and have four legs. Each leg ends with a three-fingered manipulator claw; the rear legs can magnetically adhere to a structure while the front two use a variety of cutting and welding tools. Salvage mechs can operate under their own thrust in space and have enough propellant and oxygen to allow a driver to work for several hours. Additional tools include x-ray scanners, a sealant foam injector the operator can use to keep from venting air when working on a sealed craft or habitat, and fire suppression gear.

Although humans have continued to refine tools for killing each other, many of the essential qualities of weapons used in the system have remained the same for centuries. Although weapons are often regulated in settled or populated areas, out in the expanse, it is usually wise to have a weapon close at hand. More detailed weapon information can be found on the following pages. However, if you prefer a more cinematic game and aren’t concerned with the mechanical details, you can instead use the simplified information provided on the Generic Weapons table.

While many view close combat weapons as archaic, the truth is that sometimes cracking heads up close and personal is how things get done. Most modern close combat weapons tend to be batons and similar things wielded by security, or simple knives or shivs used (and often made) by those with nothing else available. The most common close combat weapon remains the empty hand or closed fist, and characters with the Self-Defense Style and Striking Style talents have some advantages in unarmed combat (see Chapter 3).

LIGHT WEAPONS Light weapons tend to be quick and easy to wield, lending themselves to a fast and agile fighting style. They include things like batons or similar short clubs, knives and short or light blades, light staff weapons (like the bo staff), knuckle-dusters like brass knuckles, and so forth. Light weapons can add either the wielder’s Dexterity or Strength score as a modifier to damage, depending on how they’re wielded.

HEAVY WEAPONS Heavy weapons rely much more on strength to wield, ranging from a sledgehammer or other heavy tool to literally “getting medieval” on an opponent with a heavy sword, axe, or similar weapon. Heavy weapons do more damage but are limited to adding the wielder’s Strength score instead of Dexterity.

MAKESHIFT WEAPONS Characters sometimes use objects not intended or designed for combat as makeshift weapons, ranging from a piece of construction rebar to a tool case or a heavy mug from a galley. When a character uses a makeshift weapon, the GM may apply one or more of the following flaws: Fragile, Ineffective, or Poor. See Item Qualities and Flaws earlier in this chapter for details.

STUNNING WEAPONS Some weapons are designed specifically to incapacitate without wounding their targets, particularly useful for security personnel or even civilians, as stunning weapons tend to be permitted for personal defense more than lethal weaponry. They include things like handheld stunners and stun pistols, which use charges of electricity, or close range chemical weapons like mace or pepper spray. As a general guideline, a stunning weapon does penetrating damage (see Penetrating Damage in Chapter 5) but inflicts one die less damage than a comparable lethal weapon, so stun pistols do 1d6 damage versus pistols which do 2d6, for example. A target taken out by the damage from a stunning weapon cannot have the dying condition applied to them, since such weapons aren’t lethal. See Taken Out under Applying Damage in Chapter 5 for more.

Weapon Capacity

Guns have limited amounts of ammunition and are subject to mechanical problems like jamming. During gameplay, rather than having to track every round fired, you can use the following guideline to handle things like misfires, jams, and running out of ammo. When an attack with a gun misses, and the number on the Drama Die is a 6, then the weapon has jammed or run out of ammo. Reloading the gun or clearing the problem takes a major action. The Rapid Reload stunt can reduce this time, as can some talents. If a character is using non-standard ammo, that ammunition type is fully depleted. The weapon must be reloaded, but that type of ammo cannot be used until more can be acquired, either by purchasing it or obtaining more from storage. Standard ammo is considered to be part of upkeep and does not need to be paid for; however, non-standard ammo requires an Income test. The GM can also have a gun jam or run out of ammo as a minor effect of the Churn, or the weapon cannot be cleared or reloaded (because the character has no more ammo) as a major effect. See The Churn in the Game Mastering chapter for additional details.

In addition to the regular qualities listed for equipment under Item Qualities and Flaws, ranged weapons can have the following additional qualities.

BIOMETRICALLY LINKED The weapon is keyed to a specific user, or perhaps a small number of users, preventing anyone else from using it. This precaution is commonly taken in high security facilities such as prisons. The link can take several forms, including a palmprint reader, voice analyzer, or retina scanner.

CONCEALABLE Due to compact size, collapsible sections, or something similar, the weapon can be hidden under clothing and isn’t glaringly obvious when carried. This grants a +2 bonus to any tests made to conceal the item, such as Dexterity (Stealth) to sneak it past a guard.

AUTOMATIC The weapon reloads and fires automatically so long as its trigger is depressed. This makes the weapon capable of performing stunts with the (Automatic) quality on the Gun Stunts table in Chapter 5.

HIGH CAPACITY The weapon carries a substantial amount of ammunition. Ignore the first roll indicating the weapon has run out of ammo (see Weapon Capacity on the previous page).

LONG RANGE The weapon’s effective ranges are doubled. See Range under Making Attacks in Chapter 5 for details.

RECOILLESS Many slugthrowers have a recoilless variant designed for use in zero-g or microgravity situations. They fire self-propelled rounds that look rather like miniature rockets—which, in essence, they are. Recoilless guns inflict the same damage as the equivalent standard gun—and can have the same qualities and flaws, including different types of ammunition—but the cost is increased by 2 points. Most recoilless guns have the Unreliable flaw. In atmosphere, recoilless rounds leave a trail of exhaust, granting a gun firing them the Tracer ammunition quality.

SPREADING The weapon fires a spreading cone of pellets, shot, or similar small ammunition, like a shotgun. It does one die less damage but can hit all targets within a roughly 30-degree angle in front of the shooter.

Non-Standard Ammo

In addition to the regular qualities listed for equipment under Item Qualities and Flaws and the existing Ranged Weapon Qualities, different non-standard ammo types can be purchased that effectively grant a quality to that firearm for as long as the ammo lasts. When non-standard ammo is used, it lasts until a miss with a 6 on the Drama Die is rolled (see Weapon Capacity) or the end of an adventure. Non-standard ammo can be restocked or repurchased during an Interlude.

ANTI-PERSONNEL These rounds are geared toward harming soft targets (such as people), with the side effect of inflicting less harm to hard targets (including objects and armored combatants). Targets wearing armor have their armor bonus increased by +2 against attacks by anti-personnel rounds, but the damage inflicted on a successful attack is 2 points higher than a normal attack for that type of weapon. Anti-Personnel weapons cannot also have the Non-lethal quality.

ARMOR-PIERCING The weapon’s rounds reduce the Toughness bonus of worn armor by −2 in terms of reducing their damage. Unfortunately, armor-piercing rounds also have the ability to punch through vacuum-sealed bulkheads, so a missed attack with one on a spaceship or station near an outside wall may cause a hull breach. On a miss, roll 1d6; on a roll of 1 or 2, a breach occurs and the air begins rushing out of the compartment. See the Threats chapter for details on suffocation hazards.

HIGH-EXPLOSIVE HE rounds contain an explosive material that detonates on impact, intended to provide an extra punch against hard targets. Against a high-explosive attack’s damage, the target’s Toughness is considered to be half its normal value, rounded down.

INCENDIARY Utilizing a self-oxidizing flammable gel that produces intense heat, incendiary rounds inflict an additional 1d6 damage for 2d6 rounds following the initial impact—unless someone can scrub off the gel.

LOW-SHRAPNEL These high-impact plastic rounds are designed to flatten when they hit hard targets, intended as a safety precaution so they don’t blow holes in the hull of a ship or habitat. A side effect of this is that wearers of medium armor or heavier have their armor bonus increased by +2 against this type of ammo. Combatants familiar with this ammo often use a Ricochet Gun Stunt to bounce this kind of round off surfaces and into targets not in line-of-sight.

Grenades

Unlike attacks with ranged weapons that must be aimed, you don’t need to score a direct hit on a target with a grenade or other explosive device—just get close enough to catch them in the blast. Most grenades are highly illegal within space habitats, with even military forces limiting themselves to flash and smoke only. Thrown grenades are ranged weapons with a short range of 4 meters and a long range of 8 meters. Use the Ready action to have the grenade in your hand, and then you take a Ranged Attack action to throw it. Grenade launchers load and fire grenades automatically and don’t require a Ready action, but they’re subject to running out of grenades or jamming, as described under Weapon Capacity. The range for a grenade launcher can be found on the Weapon Range table in Chapter 5.

Throwing Grenades

A grenade attack is a TN 11 Accuracy (Thrown) test, modified for difficult throws at the GM’s discretion. Success means the grenade lands and detonates where you intended, but failure means the grenade lands up to 1d6 meters away in the direction of the GM’s choosing and then explodes. Grenades have area of effect (listed under the grenade’s description). Targets within range of the first area of effect number take full damage. Those within range of the second area of effect number take half damage. You can use action stunts with grenade attacks. Each stunt can affect only one target, but you need not assign all stunts to the same target. If you catch two foes in the blast of a grenade and generate 4 SP, for example, you could use Overcome Toughness on one foe and Knock Prone on the other. Humanity has developed numerous variants of the grenade. These can be represented by applying a special quality to the standard grenade.

Optional Rule: You vs. Grenades

Grenades are terrifying weapons capable of serious destruction. Here are some optional maneuvers characters can employ against them, if the GM allows. Note that characters can only exercise one of these options against a single grenade attack, except in the rare event that one doesn’t go off for a round or longer, but they can attempt these out of the normal turn sequence.

FALL ON IT

You may protect allies by covering a grenade with your body. The grenade inflicts double damage to you, but anyone else nearby only suffers half damage, and only within the first area of effect listed. (If you are wearing powered armor or the equivalent, those nearby take no damage.) You can fall on any grenade that lands adjacent to you with a successful TN 13 Willpower (Self-Discipline or Faith) test. This uses up your next minor action (even if it takes place next round) and renders you prone—if it matters. Only one person can attempt this action per grenade.

SEEK COVER

You can attempt to leap for cover if it’s within 2 meters of you, gaining the benefits of cover versus grenades. You can also drop prone to reduce a grenade’s damage by 1d6, but only if you’re outside the first listed area of effect. This requires a successful TN 15 Dexterity (Initiative) test, indicating you ducked for cover in time. This uses up your next minor action, even if that takes place next round.

THROW IT BACK

Instead of seeking cover, you can throw grenade that lands within 2 meters somewhere else if you succeed at a TN 17 Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) test. If you succeed, however, you may make an immediate attack with Accuracy (Grenades). This uses up your next major action, even if that takes place next round.

Medium-Scale Explosives

Medium-scale explosives include fuel ignitions and some missiles. Fuel-ignition weapons don’t explode, instead creating a swift and deadly patch of fire. Characters can throw makeshift fuel-ignition weapons, like Molotov cocktails. Molotov cocktails and other bottle bombs have the same automatic range as thrown grenades, but instead of exploding, they ignite into billowing fireballs that are major hazards. They deal 3d6 penetrating damage every round across an area with a 5-meter radius, which expands by 2 meters in every direction each round. Characters can make a TN 11 Perception (Seeing) test to notice the incoming bottle bomb before it lands and a TN 13 Dexterity (Acrobatics) test to get out of the initial incendiary radius if they do notice, halving the damage. In an enclosed space like a moving vehicle, add +1 to the Acrobatics test’s TN. Fuel-ignition weapons are highly illegal on space habitats because, in addition to their potential to damage the delicate physical infrastructure, burning materials also rapidly deplete breathable atmosphere. See Suffocation in the Threats chapter for details on what might happen if the fire from one of these weapons is not extinguished rapidly. Characters can use the Rupture Vehicle Combat stunt to cause fuel-ignition explosions. Shooting a stand-alone tank of fuel causes it to explode, creating a major hazard that deals 3d6 penetrating damage within a 5-meter radius, expanding by 2 meters in every direction each round.

Large-Scale Explosives

Large scale explosives include charges, timed bombs, and some missiles. These are the kinds of explosives a character can use to take down a whole building or collapse a tunnel. A character can set timed bombs or charges ahead of time and then detonate them later with a remote detonator. Both consist of explosive materials packed into forms that are safe to handle. Setting charges and bombs requires a TN 15 Intelligence (Explosives) test; failing to set them properly could result in meaningless collateral damage that doesn’t have the intended effect or could put the saboteurs themselves in mortal danger. To bring down a whole building, a bridge, or some other large target, charges must be placed in strategic locations designed to bring down the structure’s foundations. It is also possible to attach explosive charges to drones and fly them to a target. Setting these charges works as above, though directing them to a moving target requires an Intelligence (Technology) test opposed by the highest of each target’s Perception (Seeing or Hearing or Intuition)—instead of the Intelligence (Explosives) test for planting stationary charges—to inflict full damage on the intended target(s). The quantity of explosive material determines the hazard category, the toughest kind of material it can destroy, and how large the area of effect is; these quantities are measured by the difficulty of the Income test it takes to acquire them. Damage from these explosives is split evenly between standard and penetrating. The GM may allow a Dexterity (Acrobatics) test to halve the damage someone takes if they’re in range, which could represent diving out a window or taking heavy cover. People and unmoored objects in range go flying a significant distance in addition to taking damage and may end up buried under piles of debris, requiring help to escape. Note that the damage they take from the concussive impact is included in the base damage unless they happen to also fall a long distance, which is handled as its own separate hazard. Missiles (self-guided), rockets (self-propelled but unguided), and torpedoes (missiles designed to function underwater) fired from a vehicle or a surface-to-air (SAM) launcher are all at the murderous hazard tier of the Explosives Cost Difficulty table. They cause this hazard whether the tests made to fire them succeed or not; it’s just a matter of whether they destroy the target they were meant to destroy.

When expecting combat, characters may make use of protective armor, although wearing armor also sends a signal that you are expecting a fight. While padding or light armor may escape notice, especially in the rough-and-tumble places of the Belt, medium and heavy armor tends to be restricted to military, police, and security personnel on-duty and, even then, to personnel who are prepared for a fight. Waltzing onto the docks of a station in full armor is sure to get station security wondering what kind of trouble you are expecting—or looking for.

Armor Details

Armor in The Expanse has two traits: its armor bonus, which is an increase in the wearer’s Toughness, and an armor penalty, which represents the armor’s bulk and restriction and applies as a penalty to the wearer’s Dexterity and Speed.

Lastly, the table lists the usual Income target number to purchase that type of armor. Note that most armor above ballistic cloth may be restricted to military and licensed security personnel and thus only available on the black market to anyone lacking membership in those groups.

Armor Qualities and Flaws

Qualities particular to armor in The Expanse include Effective (increased armor bonus), Impressive, and Light (reduced armor penalty). Common armor flaws include Heavy, Poor, and Shoddy, reducing the armor’s overall effectiveness.

Place-Specific Armor Qualities & Flaws

Because of differences in both usage and origin, armor produced in different parts of the Sol system frequently reflect those origins in their qualities and flaws. Martian armor has a reputation for being well made, often accompanied by the Effective quality. Earth armor is often more elaborately made, reflecting the resource wealth of the human homeworld, and may grant the Impressive or Fine quality. In the Belt, quality armor is harder to come by but often tailored to a specific niche, frequently imparting both the Shoddy flaw and the Favored Stunt quality. The following specific qualities also reflect differences in armor use in varying environments.

CAMOUFLAGE Armor can be painted to make the wearer more difficult to notice or target in a specific type of environment. Common camo patterns include green and brown for Terrestrial wilderness, gray and beige for urban settings (including habitat interiors), shades of red that match the Martian surface, and the mottled gray and white common on several populated moons (including Luna and Ganymede). Camouflage grants a +2 bonus to Dexterity (Stealth) tests made in a matching environment.

GRAVITY SPECIFIC The armor is intended for use in one gravity type (such as microgravity or normal gravity) and is unwieldy in others. Sometimes this is due to the materials used—a thicker material that makes for good padded armor on Ceres might be heavier than equivalent armor on Earth. In other cases, the armor’s basic purpose might not translate well to other environments, such as armor intended to protect combat troops during high-g maneuvers on the way to a battle zone. This specificity makes the armor cheaper to produce (reducing the Income test by 2) but applies an additional −1 armor penalty when used in gravity types other than the one for which it was made.

Shields are essentially handheld cover against attacks, providing the user with a bonus to Defense rather than armor rating. Any attack that misses the character due to the Defense bonus can be assumed to have glanced off the shield.

Power Armor

One of the most fearsome sights on the battlefield is military power armor, like the Goliath suits worn by Martian Marines. Two and a half meters tall, and weighing 400 kilograms even before a soldier climbs inside, power armor provides both a formidable offense and defense. Half armor and half spacesuit, the armor has radiation shielding sufficient to let soldiers walk through a nuclear bomb crater minutes after the blast. The armor’s titanium and ceramic-composite exterior shielding is typically painted with camouflage patterns appropriate to the assignment, and enemies are often surprised just how well an enormous soldier in power armor can blend into the environment when they stand still. The armor’s hydraulics system magnifies the wearer’s strength much like a mech rig and carries most of the weight of the suit, allowing soldiers in power armor to undertake marathon hikes and move surprisingly fast. They also allow the armor to carry heavy weaponry, typically a rotary machine gun and sometimes a grenade launcher or micro-missile pack. Sensor packages feed data to the wearer on the helmet’s HUD, allowing them to identify and track infrared targeting lasers used by opponents’ weapons, and even visually parse those weapons using the suit’s camera feeds to match them against an internal database. Those same cameras monitor in all directions, sending feeds back to squad officers and their military command center, which can monitor the life signs of both the soldiers and opponents who have been detected and attacked. Despite all these capabilities, power armor is still designed for maneuverability in tight spaces, enabling infantry to move in microgravity and storm their way through the narrow confines of ships. Less so, however, is the newest addition to the Martian arsenal: 4-meter tall, 9-ton combat mechs, walking tanks carrying rail guns and missiles adapted from ship weapon systems. They are strictly ground-assault troops, so their deployment is rather limited, but there are few installations or opponents able to stand against them for long. In The Expanse game terms, power armor grants the wearer the benefits listed below. If power armor loses power, it becomes massive deadweight, effectively leaving the wearer restrained and unable to use any of the armor’s systems. Power armor requires regular maintenance activities during interludes to remain in full working order (see Interludes in Chapter 5).

As detailed in Chapter 2, Expanse characters have an Income rating measuring their overall financial resources and buying power. In the System, most financial transactions are handled electronically, and most credits—the standard of currency are recorded and stored online. Of course, there are still instances where forms of “hard” currency are in use, such as bearer bonds, bank notes, or corporate script. Some of a character’s assets may also be tied up in property or trade goods of various sorts. Different governments, and even corporations, issue their own currency as well, and exchange rates are set by various market factors. Barter is also still in use on the fringes of civilization. Among other things, barter, trade, and hard currency do not leave data trails and transactions records, which is important to some individuals. Generally, the ins and outs of various means of exchange in The Expanse are background color, to be used by the players and the GM to liven up descriptions and perhaps explain things like momentary “shortages” when an Income check fails—or when prices unexpectedly climb. The GM can also use these elements as key parts of a story, such as tracking down transactions made entirely in hard currency, a sudden surge in counterfeit currency on a station or settlement, bargains struck in currencies other than standard credits, or the crew’s reward turning out to be corporate script or some other asset rather than a direct credit deposit to their accounts. How do they convert their newfound resources into easily spendable credit without losing too much of its value? You can use the Selling Things guidelines in Chapter 2 for these situations.

A character’s Income ensures a certain lifestyle, living at a particular level of accommodation, diet, entertainment, and common “household” possessions. Lifestyle is largely determined by Income score, as given in Chapter 2 and described here.

IMPOVERISHED - INCOME −2 TO 0 The character’s circumstances are difficult, involving cramped, often makeshift living arrangements and scavenging for necessities like food and clean water. Spending on anything else is pretty much out of the question, although some people at this level find ways to acquire drugs or alcohol to numb their situation. If a character spends more than a month in this lifestyle, the GM may impose an ongoing fatigued condition—and the inability to recover from it—to reflect the rigors of it.

BASIC - INCOME 1 TO 2 This is the subsistence level of much of Earth’s population, consisting of a small apartment or the equivalent for housing, essential nutrition provided by bulk foodstuffs that don’t vary much in quality or flavor, and access to online entertainment and information channels and a steady, if not lavish, supply of legal recreational drugs. Clothing is pre-fabricated and as utilitarian as everything else. Getting around is limited to public transportation and personal possessions are few and far between.

MIDDLE CLASS - INCOME 3 TO 5 A modest lift out of the doldrums of Basic to an Income level where some personalization of one’s lifestyle is possible. This includes slightly better or larger living quarters, maybe in a better area of the character’s choice, a greater variety of food with the possibility of occasionally patronizing restaurants, and some personal possessions of significance. Owning a vehicle outside of one required for work is still relatively rare.

AFFLUENT - INCOME 6 TO 8 A noticeable amount of creature comforts, what people at the impoverished or basic levels think of as luxury, including possibly owning a house or some land or the equivalent in a dome or station off-Earth, a varied diet including a number of fresh foods, and little, if any, concern over small day-to-day purchases. The character can afford to enjoy regular entertainment, from nights-out to catered nights-in, albeit not every night; but easily a few times a month, maybe with the occasional trip or vacation in there.

WEALTHY - INCOME 9 TO 10 Most of the expenses that concern middle class and lower people don’t worry the wealthy at all. They have sufficient Income or expense accounts to largely live where they want, to eat what they want when they want it, and to enjoy most of what the world has to offer. At this level, a personal vehicle of some kind of common, and wealthy characters may even have multiple homes, or one fairly lavish one.

RICH - INCOME 11 TO 13 The truly rich concern themselves with very little, except the opinions and goodwill of their peers (if that). This income ensures personal quarters that would accommodate multiple families on Basic, and luxuries they could not afford with more than a year’s Income. The rich have all of the benefits of the wealthy and then some, including perhaps some significant quasi-legal ones.

VERY RICH - INCOME 14 OR GREATER It’s difficult for lower-income characters to entirely conceive of this lifestyle, which often throws away and recycles more than the lower-level lifestyles ever own. Characters living the very rich lifestyle live in mansions or even palaces (or their equivalent), usually with a staff of personnel to attend to their needs. They move freely using personal vehicles, including their own orbital lifters and spacecraft.

Living Above Your Means

Generally, characters who maintain their income can live at its lifestyle level indefinitely without any need for a test, so long as they put in the work, barring some misfortune. Still, there are those occasions when a character wants or needs something that’s routinely beyond their reach, either a specific purchase or just an opportunity to enjoy a taste of the good life (or, at least, a better life). When characters look to live above their means, use the following guidelines. The character makes an Income check with a difficulty of the minimum income for the increase lifestyle +9. So , for example, a character wanting to gain a benefit of the affluent lifestyle would test Income against TN 15 (9 + the minimum Income for affluent). This depletes the character’s income, as described under Depleting Income in Chapter 2. Thus, living above your means for any length of time will rapidly decrease a character’s income. If the test succeeds, the character gains the benefit of that lifestyle, whether it is a lavish party, a personal item (ranging from a piece of jewelry or clothing to personal electronics or a household item), or a temporary improvement in living conditions. Since living above your means depletes your Income, it may mean the character’s lifestyle for the following month drops; for example, if Income is depleted from 6 to 5, the character drops from affluent to middle class lifestyle. This may means some belt-tightening until the character’s Income recovers. If the character wants to maintain the higher lifestyle, then that’s another Income test, which further depletes Income, leading to a potentially rapid decline. At the GM’s discretion, a short-term windfall (see the Rewards chapter) may temporarily grant the benefits of living at a higher lifestyle until the windfall is depleted and the character returns to the regular lifestyle level determined by their Income.

Food is a constant human need, and because complex biologicals (digestible by humans) originate only on Earth, humanity has been forced to adapt. The simplest foodstuffs are wheat pastes mixed with honey or spices for flavor and dried fruit for texture, which is familiar to anyone who has tongued it out of a helmet-tube while working in an environment suit. It’s also enticing to those looking for nothing more than the simplest of fuels for their body. Equally infamous is the Martian Navy’s “slop,” a heated high-protein, high-carb food mix. Textured proteins derived from soy and mushrooms take all kinds of forms from fake eggs to fake cheese and fake bacon to fake steak. Belters are used to different kinds of “kibble,” protein pellets or crumbles with seasonings and flavor sauces, or versions of noodle bowls or similar food. Better food is available, but its price scales with its quality. Vat-grown meat is said to be as good as the real thing—though few truly believe it. Microgravity fish farms produce shrimp, salmon, and other seafood well suited for microgravity. Hydroponic rigs are common, from family-scale up to the industrial, but fresh strawberries still command a fair price. Mushrooms and myco-proteins are a staple, easily grown and fertilized with organic waste. Among the rarest of foods is real cheese, worth more per ounce than precious metals out in the Belt, leading to a thriving black market. Beverages vary just as much as food, both in type and quality. A common late-night argument is whether or not it’s truly safe to drink ice-melt straight from Saturn, but the debate doesn’t keep Belter miners from doing it when needed. Others prefer the water after it’s been run through their particular local set of filters. Those who claim particularly refined sense of taste seek out pricy water with clarity and taste improved through lengthy filtration and remineralization using tweaked versions of the same systems used to provide precise water-mineral balance to high-end hydroponics. Even if they are indifferent about water, everybody has their preferences when it comes to liquor. Nearly every ship and station where the rules allow (and most where they can be bent) has stills and distilleries turning out a wide variety of beer and wine from cheap and terrible to the surprisingly good. Drinks like fungal-culture whiskey started as desperate experiments and exploded into full-grown industries, and tweaks to recipes for pseudotequila and cheap Belter scotch are regularly traded while passing bottles of the end product.

A “hole” on Mars. A “cabin” on an ice freighter headed toward Saturn. A “common” on a mining family’s ship out past Anderson Station. There are an infinite variety of places space-going humanity calls home, but they have much in common. First and foremost, every cubic meter of space humans make into a home has to be claimed from a hostile environment and then defended from it. On a planet like Mars or a planetoid like Ceres, these spaces are mined out from solid rock and their walls sealed with a coating of plastic, with tunnels off of tunnels in the warrens making up those habitats. On ships, the walls are metal, often with the ship’s water tanks just beyond providing the radiation shielding that rock does planetside. Both rock and metal walls seal in a critical bubble of air. Of course, as the saying goes “the only place air’s free is Earth”— simple greenery like snake plants and devil’s ivy are common in many homes, staples of first-generation air recycling schemes now kept as good luck charms by those hoping for the most efficient use of expensive air consumed by the home. Once claimed, a space can be made into a home. Full-spectrum LEDs provide any level of illumination from candlelight to sunlight and can be programmed to a custom cycle of both day, night, and mood lighting. Most standard designs have a tiny shower, toilet, and half-sink crammed into a tight corner, not only for space efficiency but to make it easier for water vapor to be reclaimed from the air, and allowing the remaining volume be divided up however the inhabitant desires. Sometimes utility channels allow wiring and ductwork to be hidden beyond the walls, but just as often it is attached to and painted the same color as the ceiling. For a touch of comfort or luxury, rock or metal surfaces can be given a veneer of wood-textured laminate or even a thin layer of real wood; lodge-pole pine has proven the most robust variety for growth in low gravity. Shipboard, when multiple travelers or crew share quarters, each still tends to have their own pressed-metal footlocker, with its edges magnetized to keep it stuck to deck plating during maneuvers or wall plating so it can act as a hanging cabinet. When space is particularly tight, even planetside, home furnishings take a cue from spaceships and are designed to fold against the walls. A home terminal linked to the inhabitants’ hand terminals and local memory partitions is standard. Some homes have screen walls, large high-resolution film displays covering entire walls that can mirror local data from terminals, show programming from a variety of feeds, or act as “windows” linked to cameras across the solar system. Real windows are follies on ships and stations, needless weak points and risks. Personal possessions tend to be useful or particularly valued by the inhabitants. Not every home has its own fabricator, sending the inhabitants to nearby shops or stores for their needs, but every home has a recycler to ensure as little raw matter as possible goes to waste. A separate capture and disposal system takes care of organic waste, shunting it into its own processing system. Despite sparse possessions and quick disposal of unwanted material, the end appearance is not a spartan home but one that is simple and clean. Off Earth, it takes wealth, effort, or both to live in cluttered squalor.

Most medical tech is covered under the Recovering interlude (see Interludes in Chapter 5) and the care of a physician or auto-doc. At the GM’s discretion, a character who has ongoing medical needs like blood screenings, anti-cancer meds, or other regular treatments may have a +1 or +2 increase in the Income requirement for their lifestyle to reflect the additional expense. A one-time medical expense like the replacement of a limb or organ is generally Income TN 15 to 18 or more, depending on the quality or the replacement, from a relatively inexpensive prosthetic to a newly cloned limb. When it comes to modern medicine, the question largely isn’t whether miracles are possible, but if they’re available and affordable. The need to maintain the body during long periods living in microgravity and surviving bursts of high acceleration has led to revolutions in the understanding of biology and physiology. Generations of biochemists working in microgravity have produced pharmaceuticals undreamed of before humanity left Earth, and the greatest accidental genetics experiment of all time—the rise of Belters through the influence of their environment—has given geneticists more data than even their expert systems can process. If necessity is the mother of invention, humanity’s settlement of space has placed a whole new set of demands on medical science, which has invented the means to meet them.

Pharmaceuticals

Everyone who lives and travels in space is familiar with standard medical supplements issued to encourage bone growth and density, descendants of the same drugs once allowing short duration visits to orbit, but now enabling humans to travel and live indefinitely in deep space. Similar improvements led to topical coagulation boosters which quickly staunch the flow of blood from a wound, critical for fighting blood loss in microgravity, and a variety of autophagic drugs helping control everything from fatigue to systemic cellular breakdown. Anti-cancer medications are necessary for those who have experienced significant radiation exposure due to poor shielding.

Drugs and Conditions

A primary use of pharmaceuticals is to mitigate and ease various conditions (see Conditions in Chapter 1). From amphetamine derivatives intended to ward off being fatigued and exhausted to pain-killers to shrug off the effects of being injured or wounded, and even life-saving drugs to save people from Dying, the right pharmaceutical cocktail can alleviate the effects of almost any condition, at least temporarily. The problem is that while drugs can treat the symptoms (and the game modifiers), generally only proper treatment can actually remove the underlying condition. See Recovering in the Interludes section of Chapter 5 for details.

Enhancement implants in The Expanse are anything that is engineered to change a character’s body, which can include their brain (and therefore the mind), granting them some improved or additional ability and enhancing them in some way. Such alter ations are rarely mentioned in The Expanse novels, but they do play a central role with one character, Clarissa Mao. There are also implications that they are more prevalent among certain groups or on Earth, and replacements for lost limbs are common amongst those with dangerous jobs in the Belt. Even though limb regrowth technology exists, base model cybernetic replace ments often prove to be a cheaper option. Ultimately, it is up to the Game Master and the players to decide if enhancement implants should be included in their campaign. Many implants are cybernetic or bionic: the addition of machine or artificial parts to the body or the replacement of existing body parts with artificial prosthetics, things like cybernetic limbs or sensory organs. However, brain interfacing computers are not included, as there is no evidence of true cyborgs, short for “cybernetic organism,” in The Expanse universe. In other instances, augmentations are engineered, but they take the form of things like organ transplants, genetic engineering (in vitro or using recombinant DNA and gene editing), and other biological modifications, sometimes called “wetware” or “biotech.” Protogen and other biotech companies were heavily involved in this sort of modification, which eventually became Project Caliban after the discovery of the protomolecule. Various forms of biohacking protomolecule are certainly ongoing as evidenced in the later Expanse novels and in the adventures To Sleep Perchance to Dream and Abzu’s Bounty.

The human body and mind can only be safely modified so much. The degree to which a character can be enhanced is called Capacity. A character’s Capacity score is the number of slots that can be filled with implants. Each implant “fills” one or more

Higher Starting Capacity

The starting Capacity of 0 reflects the relatively infrequent appear - ance of implants in The Expanse novels. However, if you wish to have a campaign where implants are more common, you can increase this starting value. The Game Master can set the Capacity for player characters in the campaign depending on its style and overall emphasis on enhanced implants:

  • The default for an Expanse game is low enhancement, which starts player characters at Capacity 0. Characters must improve their Capacity in order to have any implants without going over Capacity.
  • A medium enhancement campaign starts out with a default Capacity of 1 or 2. Some level of enhancement implants is common, and player characters are all expected to have one or two slots worth to start.
  • A high enhancement campaign starts out with a default Capacity of 3 or even more. Starting Capacity slots are effectively “free” and reflect the amount of enhancement implants player characters are expected to have in the setting. At the Game Master’s discretion, a character can “tradein” their unused starting Capacity for leveling improvements instead (see Advancement in Chapter 2), but only if you want there to be an incentive for “non-enchanced” characters. Otherwise, unused Capacity is simply that: potential the character hasn’t used yet. During character creation, a character can improve their Capacity in place of one or more of the benefits granted by their Background (up to 4), their Profession (up to 4), or their Drive (up to 2), as detailed in Chapter 2. The Game Master can set a limit on improved starting Capacity for player characters, depending on how prevalent enhancement implants are in the setting, ranging from 1 (augmentations are very rare) to 6 or more (augmentation is quite common).
